1: A sword cares nothing how strong your arm may be, but only whether you can add.
One right answer lands a blow, and a string of them unbroken lands a far heavier one.
A swing begun with a wrong sum meets only air, but one that falters halfway still lands with all that is behind it.
You need not go on answering until the clock runs dry. When the foe before you is nearly dead, you may strike and be done.
Wisdom is time, for the wise are never hurried, and the clock is kinder to them than to fools.
The dungeon is a harsh teacher but an honest one, and if you go deeper than you have ever been you will arrive a little wiser.
Know the beast and you will know where the meat is, for the butcher's question is always of the animal.
A carcass is no cut of meat, nor is a cut of meat a supper, and at each step you are asked what you know.
Once Cook Ding understood the ox, he no longer had to look: his knife found its own way through every ox after that.
None ever grew tough down here by fighting. The tough ones grew tough at supper, for when you cook a meal properly the body keeps a little of it for good.
Wands ask how the world works, and if you answer, the world does as it is told.
Written magic is strict in its grammar, and read wrongly it is only paper.
Nothing down here wears its true name. Philosophy is the art of asking a thing what it really is.
Prayer is help that truly comes, though how much of it comes will hang upon how well you know the old stories.
Armour remembers where it was made, and it will let you put it on if you know your way around the world.
Every ring has a past, and it will not sit on a finger that knows no history.
A lock is only a price to a thief, and most lids will open for one who understands what things cost.
Each step costs a crumb, as does each moment spent standing still, and when the crumbs run out the dungeon begins to take them out of you.
Even the boldest traveller must ask his way at times, and the dungeon keeps a page of plain answers for any who is humble enough to ask.
Stand on treasure and stoop for it, since it will not leap into a pack.
Carry more than one kind of weapon, for some hides shrug at an edge and split under a hammer.
Look at what a monster is made of before you choose what to hit it with, for things of ice and things of fire have little love for each other's company.
From a dead adventurer's journal: 'Rested an hour. Feel better. Hungry. Something is coming down the corridor.'
Stand quietly for long enough and the mind refills a drop at a time, though never while some creature is gnawing at you.
A new stair puts a little wind back in your lungs, but the same stair a second time puts back nothing.
No floor announces its traps, but a sharp eye that passes close will sometimes find them out.
Loot belongs to its floor, and if you wish for better treasure you must go farther down to find it.
A plain box holds a plain handful. The handsomer the chest the more is inside it, and the worse it will bite a clumsy thief.
Count your purse as a shopkeeper would, for each floor pays a little better than the one above it, and what is worth buying costs a fair piece of a floor.
The question that beats you today will be asked again, and then you will know it, for learning is the one treasure that the dungeon cannot take back.
You should know better than to pick up a duck in a dungeon.
Fountains ask before they give, and the water is kind to one who answers well. Answer badly and you will wish that you had stayed thirsty.
Whatever the dead loved is buried with them. Dig only if you know your way around a map, and are ready should the owner object.
An empty throne judges all who sit upon it, and it judges them by how much they know of the past.
Listen when you come somewhere new, for someone counting coins behind a wall is no ghost story, and the sound will show you the way.
A small grey trader walks the deep roads with a pack twice his size. Stand beside him and ask, and he will show what is inside it.
A trader pays little for a mystery, and his offer will improve if you tell him what the thing is before you sell it.
Coin is heavy: a king's ransom will not fit in a hero's pack, but a ruby will.
You are remembered by what you carry out of the dark. Gold is for spending, but gems and old gold plate are for keeping.
Rust and acid may take an edge, but not forever, for a smith with a file can give back what the wet took.
A trader knows what lives below his stall. Heed what he says when first you stop, and look at what he has set out for it.
When a trader has just made a sale he is in a generous mood, so bring him your old blade while he is still smiling.
On the last floor before a great beast's lair someone always sets up shop, for heroes pay best on the night before a fight.
If you have the eye to read it, a trader's price will tell you something of what is in the bottle.
Merchants talk to merchants, and if you rob one the rest will know your face.
The monks who drew the bonnacon gave it horns that curl backwards and can hurt nobody, and yet they drew the knight fleeing from its other end.
Saint Brendan once said Mass upon an island that swam away, and a pilgrim who can find himself on a chart has less to fear from solid ground.
The poorest table in the dungeon is the one most worth sitting at, but do not come to it empty-handed.
A promise made in the dark is still a promise. Those that you carry all the way down are remembered at the bottom, and those that you sell are remembered longer.
Some who weep in chains were justly chained, and mercy that never asks a single question is only a kind of haste.
A purse is never lighter than just after a stranger brushes past, but a thief who runs may yet be caught, and the dead pay all their debts.
A hunter who has skinned rabbit after rabbit knows rabbits, but one who has skinned a rabbit, a fox and a badger knows the woods.
Every corpse is a lesson to one who has the patience to read it, and from the living it is far harder to learn.
When first a blade meets a strange beast the hand learns only whether it hurt or no, but the butcher's table teaches why.
Dress for what you mean to meet: a breastplate and a shield turn the blow, a helm guards the mind, gauntlets the grip and a cloak the breath of dragons.
Two rings of the same make are two cooks at one pot, and only the better cook does any work.
Most creatures find you with their eyes and ears. Stone will hide you, but the clash of a fight carries a long way.
A sleeping creature may be crept past or struck before it wakes, but it cannot be both.
Every floor gives you time to see all of it, but if you linger long after, the dungeon sends newcomers down the stairs to learn the reason.
Look a creature over before you close with it, for a sleeper, a wanderer, a searcher and a hunter on your trail all bear themselves differently.
A copyist's desk, a surveyor's table, a brazen head: some things in the dungeon are worth a closer look, and each will answer the curious only once.
A creature that can do something terrible usually shows it, and you do well to listen when the Chronicler warns you of one.
Somewhere in the upper shafts a little fire lizard sits on a rock in the rain, where a cruel master left him, and he has learned to fear all who are bigger than he is.
Miners named a stubborn ore after the goblins they blamed for it, and Old Nickel of the upper shafts earned that name, for every nail in his hoard came off a miner who lay down to sleep.
Rain is hard on a creature that cannot make its own warmth.
Hands that have fastened a harness once remember its buckles, but a coat of a new make has new buckles to learn.
Plate is slow to buckle on. Dress between fights and not in them, though a weapon slung at your back changes hands in a moment.
Mail stops a cut and parts under a point, plate turns an edge and rings under a hammer, and a quilted coat soaks up a club.
Every ounce in a full pack is an ounce your feet must carry when something is chasing you.
A werewolf shrugs at steel until a pinch of silver dust is worked into the edge.
A flask of holy water is only water to a wolf, but dashed against the dead it burns like fire.
Bring a hammer to a pile of bones, for skeletons have no flesh to cut and little to pierce.
Never buckle on new armour while something watches, for a knight half dressed is a knight with no armour at all.
A potion that has not told you its name is a gamble, and the dungeon's dice are loaded.
A monster wears no name for you to read, but when it is slain its corpse will speak very frankly.
An acrobat cannot tumble in a breastplate, and the lighter your coat the more your own quickness counts.
A pack mule knows to the ounce what he can carry, and lets not one ounce more be laid on his back.
Old Nickel's cloak of leaves was torn from a young Bloomsaur, and whatever that kobold owns he took from someone smaller than himself.
On a creature's page, Weak To means your blow lands twice as hard; Resists, half as hard; Shrugs Off, a quarter. Hurt Most By names the metals it cannot bear.
Little John won his place in Sherwood with a quarterstaff on a narrow bridge, and Robin Hood came up out of the brook laughing.
A knight once heard Merlin groaning under a stone that a hundred men could not lift, and was told to leave it be. Merlin moved the Giants' Dance by art, not by strength.
A highwayman's pack holds bread, cheese and a twist of dried meat, and a decent cook takes what a fallen man carried, but never the man.
Rats are brave in a heap and timid alone, so meet a swarm in a corridor, where only one of them can bite you at a time.
A wolf pack will not come down a narrow passage one wolf at a time, but waits outside for you or comes round behind.
Where kobolds live, look where you step, and look twice where a kobold has just been standing.
An archer you cannot see can see you. Carry a torch and the dark will give him away, though a lit torch gives you away to all else that is in the dark.
2: Something lies asleep in the iron-caged glass sphere. Throw it gently, for you do not get to choose who wakes up.
The brighter the light inside a sphere, the more grown is the companion asleep in it, and a sphere that wears a little crown holds one already at the height of its strength.
A companion that fights beside you long enough stops being the creature you first met.
A hurt companion mends slowly by itself, faster upon your supper, and faster still upon your medicine.
You may tell a companion to follow, to hold its ground or to go hunting, but it will never guess which you wished.
Feed a companion from your own pack and it grows faster than fighting alone would make it, though your own stomach will feel the loss.
Companions fight as well as their master has been answering, and your mistakes make them clumsy too.
With the little shard of the Stone you question a thing, and if you lose it all things stay strangers to you.
Guess wrong at a thing's true name and the shard will leave you seeing stars. Never do your philosophy with a monster watching.
When you have named one thing truly you have named its whole kind, and every potion of that sort you ever meet, blessed or cursed, will tell you what it is.
Things come blessed, plain or cursed and do not say which, and the cursed ones are easy to put on.
A knight keeps one harness for the tourney and another for the road, each on its own peg, and hands that know every buckle can change them quickly.
A thing laid on an altar may confess what it is, for the altar tells the truth to the kind, lies to the cruel and says nothing to those who are neither.
Wands run dry and scrolls burn up, but a spellbook goes on teaching for as long as you go on listening.
Mana is a well that a clever head digs deeper, but do not draw the last bucket for some small thing.
Prayers are answered as far as you can carry them, for the first right answer brings a little and the last brings a great deal.
Pray anywhere and you are heard, but pray at an altar and you are heard a little better.
There are two things worth asking on your knees, mercy for the body or a steadier hand for the fight, and Heaven answers the one that you asked.
Heaven is generous but never hurried, and when one prayer has been answered it is a long walk before the next will be.
An altar hears a gift out of turn, and it lifts what is cursed before it blesses what is clean.
Jacob wrestled an angel all night and walked away with a limp and a blessing, for Heaven has always been willing to take one gift back and give another.
Nothing done in the dark is hidden from Heaven, and how you treat the helpless on the way down will be waiting for you near the bottom.
Carry a spare loaf and a spare potion, for someone down there will need them more than you, and it is noticed when you share them.
When a stranger names a price down here, it is no longer a trifle. Decide what the thing is worth before you open your purse.
Perception does not find a trap from across the room, but just before your foot does, at the only distance that matters.
Clever hands can do better than break a trap, for they can change its mind about whom it is for.
Some dishes are only supper, while others leave something of the beast in the cook, for an hour or for good.
Two things eaten are two snacks, but two things cooked together may be a recipe that nobody wrote down.
The pot asks what you know, and it gives you dinner if you know it and smoke if you guess.
How much the kitchen can do for you depends on how deep you have dared to go, so a cook who stays near the top stays small.
Nothing in your pack spoils, so goblin gristle saved on the third floor still cooks on the fortieth, into something far better than a snack.
A cook who lives by spells saves the strange parts and one who lives by the sword saves the hearty ones, and everybody eats the rest.
The great feasts ask for five things from far-apart places, and often for a part that only a great beast can give.
A locked chest asks a question of money, and if you answer it wrongly it will answer back.
A trader's first price is only where the talk begins. If you argue well it comes down, but he will not hear the same argument twice.
Learn a whole shelf of history and the dungeon stops quizzing you on it, but sums are different, for the sword never takes your word.
Blades ask the sums of their metal. Soft metal asks a child's questions, but what the deep smiths forged asks a scholar's and hits far harder for the trouble.
Armour from deep down asks of farther lands, and a helm that you cannot answer for is only a heavy hat.
The old wives knew their metals, choosing silver for what ought to be dead and cold iron for the Fair Folk.
Whatever lands on the shield is a blow you never have to heal.
Armour is less a wall than an argument, and even the best of it loses now and then.
Scratched low on a wall, in a shaky hand: 'The vine does not chase you, and it had no need to chase me.'
Every so often the dungeon stops being rooms and becomes a maze, and every so often after that the stairs have an owner.
To see a monster is not to know it, but its body will tell you everything if you know how to ask.
A wand that reads a creature's make teaches as much as a corpse on the table, though the creature is left alive to resent it.
First you know a family by sight and then by the signs it leaves on a stair, but its weaknesses come later, and only to the patient.
Those who die down here do not always leave, for some stay to guard what they carried, and they no longer know their old friends.
I know I shouldn't pick up that duck... but what if...
Certain altars want a gift before they will listen, and the gift is never far, so search the other rooms before you give up.
The alchemists swore that lead could be made into gold with patience and a little philosophy, and one of their crucibles is waiting down here still.
The Welsh told of a cauldron that would not boil a coward's food, but the one down here is more hungry than particular.
Nicholas of Myra threw his gold through a window at night that none might thank him, and the ledger of gifts marks the unsigned ones.
Lions remember longer than men, as Androcles learned before the eyes of all Rome.
The Watch never stops waiting for a dispatch, and a sealed case is dead weight only until it meets the right sergeant.
The quick are missed more often than the armoured are spared, and past a point nimble feet do what more plate cannot.
Plate sits light on strong shoulders, but on weak ones every link drags at the feet and gives the monsters an extra moment.
Quick hands strike twice while a slow beast strikes once, and in the lightest coat they may be as quick as they truly are.
Some purses are held out so that someone may watch you take them. Turning down a thing you could have taken, because taking it would be wrong, is seen even when nobody is looking.
To help is not the same as to be good. A kindness given blind may cost you dearly, and it buys nothing upon the scales.
Some cold spots are no draught. When a blow comes out of empty air, walk into the air and you will find what threw it.
Some slimes are only multiplied by a sword. Ask what the blade will make before you swing it.
Owning up costs something, or it is only talk. Say 'it was me' to the face of the one you wronged and pay back what you can, and the scales will notice.
Salt serves for the restless, cold iron for the Fair Folk and a polished shield for the gorgon, and a hunter who truly knows a family reaches for its old trick without stopping to think.
A hoard asleep is still a hoard watched. Take a little, walk softly, and be gone before something counts the coins.
A wolf follows your scent where eyes would lose you, for invisibility is nothing to a nose.
Snakes and spiders feel your footsteps through the stone, but if you stand still they lose you.
A hunter that loses you goes to where it last saw you, looks about and gives up, so give it time and keep quiet.
A dagger is a poor weapon in a fair fight, but no one has said that the fight must be fair, or that your foe must be awake.
Below the Labyrinth each stretch of the dungeon keeps dangers of its own, and most may be seen by any who looks before he steps.
When one family holds a floor, it pays to know that family.
The dungeon's odd corners pay the curious in knowledge, coin, a meal or a draught, but never in armour, for it rewards curiosity and not greed.
A carved lintel with an owl on it marks a door that was never meant to be found, and it will open if you answer it.
A war-band fights for its leader. When you have brought him down, see how brave the rest of them remain.
Some creatures muddle the mind if they draw close, and those are best fought from a distance, with a bow, a wand or a thrown spear.
Watch the walls in Asterion's maze, for where he walks through one it cracks and dust falls.
Fire is the answer to a swarm, for a blade kills two beetles and misses ten thousand.
Holy power burns the dead and the damned, but against an honest bear a blessed blade is only a blade.
The golem of Prague woke when a word was written on its brow, and lay down for good when a single letter of it was rubbed away.
The dead have already done all the sleeping they will ever need.
Rust eats iron and steel, but leather, wood and bronze it leaves alone.
Iron carries the lightning straight to the skin and leather goes up like kindling, while dragonscale lets fire run off it but stiffens in the frost.
Thieves have good reason to wear leather, for a knight in plate cannot sidestep a blow and every sleeper in the hall hears him coming.
A fencer who lunges leaves his chest open, and one who waits behind his blade strikes softly. Choose which to be in the fight before you.
A greatsword held in both hands turns blows aside as a small shield would.
Beasts and trolls are afraid of fire, and a troll cannot close a burn as it closes a cut.
Viper venom on an edge does nothing to the dead, who have no blood left to carry it.
Greek fire won sea battles for Byzantium, and though it is less grand when thrown from your own hand, it is still fire.
A smith can beat a sword into a mace and keep both metal and blessing, so a good blade that no longer suits the fight need not stay a sword.
Silver worked into a blade makes it a silver blade in the eyes of any werewolf, and cold iron does the same against the Fair Folk.
Salamander's wool will not burn, and an armourer who keeps some can line your cloak with it before you go where some beast breathes fire.
Pay a smith now and he can make what he does not have on his rack, to be yours when you meet him farther down the road.
A smith will not put his hammer to a metal he cannot name, any more than a cook will season a pot he has not tasted.
Heracles carried the golden apples a long way and Atalanta stopped running for them, yet some fruit does more in a pot than in a pocket.
An archer you can see cannot hurt you while the Galdr of the Stayed Spear holds.
Seal the healer's mouth first, for a silenced foe cannot wail, sing, summon or heal.
3: Companions grow from time at your side, from the fights you share, from your supper and from a kind word, and none of these alone is enough.
After its first great change a companion learns a trick of its own, and it will show you, if you ask.
A companion called back into its sphere is not gone. Throw the sphere again and the same friend steps out, bearing the same name.
Your companion is jealous of your attention, and if you wake another the first goes back to sleep in its own sphere, safe in your pack.
Watch where your companion will not step. It can smell a curse lying on the floor, which is more than you can do.
A thing's true name comes all at once, curse and strength and story together, or it does not come at all.
Spells have shapes, a line or a fan or a burst. Know which you hold before you decide where to stand.
Two enemies who fight each other are two fewer fighting you, and there is magic that can arrange it.
Feast a little on every floor rather than a great deal on one, for only so much building can be done on a body in one place.
A simple stew of shallow things can raise a gift of the body only so high, for the deep creatures teach what the shallow cannot.
Take a trap apart perfectly and it gives up more than its spring, for the dungeon pays its best tinkers in secrets.
A trap that you rewire will be loyal to you only once.
Heaven hears a whisper from the bottom of a well better than a shout from the top of a tower.
From clean hands the same prayer is worth more and from dirty ones less, and an altar makes the difference plainer.
Start early, for at the bottom it is no single deed that is weighed, but the whole road.
Plain metals come first, and after them metals with names out of stories. When a weapon's sums grow suddenly hard, look again at what it is made of.
The horned king walks through the walls of his own maze, which is hardly fair. Yet a princess of Crete once handed a stranger a small thing that was no sword, and by it the contest was made fair.
No blade could pierce the lion that Heracles strangled, and so he wore its hide ever after, though it is not so good on a man as it was on the lion.
Golden thread seems a poor thing to carry into a monster's house, but Theseus would have paid dearly for a second spool.
Minos owed the sea a bull and kept it for himself. A bronze one in your pack is the same debt, and it can still be paid in water.
Asterion forgives a traveller who never learned to cook, but nothing below him will.
Count the pillars before you count on your courage, for her gaze crosses a whole hall but cannot go round a corner.
Three old sisters shared one eye between them and lost it. It is of no use for seeing with, but returned to the right hands it is of great use.
Perseus carried his polished shield on his arm, for he would have looked a fool with it strapped to his luggage.
Medusa cannot harm what cannot see her, and a strip of cloth, though a desperate answer, is an answer still.
No quest for a great stair is finished on the floor where it begins. Carry strange things downward, for somebody below is waiting for them.
Each great stair has an owner with a name, and with each name comes an old story of how the owner died, to be read before you knock.
Any gatekeeper can be beaten the hard way, and a few of those who tried it have even lived to tell of it.
Shovels make poor weapons until something heavy walks over the ground that they dug.
Sigurd did not think of the pit by himself, but had it from an old one-eyed stranger. Take your advice from the same quarter.
Read before you sharpen, for every creature that you have truly studied has a page in your book that says what hurts it.
The dungeon notices habits, be it one weapon kept faithfully, one mistake survived again and again or one prayer made at every threshold, and enough of any habit earns it a name.
Those you meet down here are not all selling the same thing, for some sell goods and some sell stories, and some are buying you.
When a bargain feels too rich at the moment it is offered, ask who profits if you say yes.
If you find something that plainly belonged to someone, you may expect to meet that someone a little farther down.
Burdens taken up for a stranger cannot always be set down again, but an altar can break what hands cannot.
There are touches that take a piece of you which supper will not put back, and a strong body throws them off more often than a weak one.
A rattled head still knows the answer, but has less time in which to say it.
A healing draught does not care how big you have grown, for it mends the giant as well as it mends the boy.
A fight carries far, and whatever comes down the stair while it still rings within earshot will go to see what the noise was.
Read the first line you are given on a new floor, for sometimes it is a warning of who lives there, though it never gives a name.
The box that says 'Do not open' has a very good lock on it, and none who picked it cleanly has ever found Hope inside.
Odin paid for his drink at the well before he tasted it, and no one ever offered to give him back the eye.
Percival sat at the wounded king's table and was too polite to ask what ailed him, and he was not invited twice.
The Sphinx of the deep has more patience than her sister at Thebes and asks several riddles, each harder than the last, but she forgives no wrong answer.
One missed stroke of the bellows spoils a dwarf-smith's work, and the unfinished hammer-head waits for one who can keep count.
A king's seal found loose in the dungeon opens no door, but it earns a hearing before an empty judgment seat, where the questions are of the past.
The Fleece hung in a grove at Colchis under a serpent that never slept, and it is of beasts that the serpent wishes to hear.
In a roofless chapel stands a bare altar, with a ring worn into the stone where a cup once stood. Bring the cup, and know your scripture.
The unicorn of the old tapestries could never be hunted down. She came of her own accord, and only to the gentle and the patient.
Unicorns know what kind of traveller stands before them, and they do not look twice at the cruel.
Blades skidded off the Boar of Calydon, until Atalanta's arrow went in and Meleager's spear after it, and that spear was kept.
In Utgard no contest is what it seems, and though Thor lost all three he frightened his host badly by how nearly he won.
You become what you eat, so before you cook the beast ask what the beast was good at.
One good meal is a promise, and a second a floor later is that promise kept.
Stillness refills the mind, but each floor holds only so much quiet. A keener mind draws more of it, and the next floor has quiet of its own.
A spell is a key and no hammer. Find the lock it was cut for and it opens the fight, though your own arithmetic still has to finish it.
Nerve is more than one brave moment. Hold firm when the hard questions come, and hold firm again a long way farther down, for it is the second time that shows what you are.
If you give a stranger what he asks before you know what he is, you may pay for it in blood, in coin or in another's grief.
The one-eyed giant and the many-eyed horror see what is really there. Eat as they saw, and for a while so will you.
Elisha's servant saw nothing until his eyes were opened and he beheld the hills full of chariots, and some draughts open eyes a little way.
Men who grew from dragon's teeth trust nobody, not even each other, so a stone thrown among them starts a fine argument.
When you know a family well enough, you will feel its kind on a floor the moment you step off the stair.
The restless dead feel the warmth of the living, even through a wall.
Giants and trolls smell the blood of a man, as the old rhyme warned in all earnest.
In the Forgotten Temple the cracked flagstones will not take much weight, and the vines hold whatever walks into them.
Count before you cross the fire vents of the Scorched Deep, for they breathe on a beat and glow white the turn before.
A necromancer's dead are bound to him, and if you end him they fall where they stand.
Know a war-band's family and you will know its make-up before you ever see its camp.
Fafnir's breath scorches the stone it crosses. The marks show you where not to stand.
Plain ring iron is the cold iron of the old stories, which the Fair Folk will not touch, and their glamour slides off a coat of it.
Perseus never once looked at the Gorgon, but watched her in his shield.
Odysseus's crew rowed past the Sirens with wax in their ears and heard nothing at all, which was both the purpose and the price.
Country people kept a nail of cold iron about them, for the Fair Folk cannot abide it.
A mirror makes a poor wall, and Perseus carried one for a single fight that he chose with care.
A wizard in iron finds his words come hard, but the dwarves' true-silver, the orichalcum of Atlantis and cloth the gods wove do not stand in his way.
Glass made harder than steel is glass still, and any smith can tell you what a hammer does to it.
Fire oil on a blade makes every cut a burn, and a troll remembers a burn long after it has forgotten the cut.
Aqua regia, the royal water, eats gold itself, and you may guess what it does to a hide.
If your blows only tickle, the fault may lie in the blade and not in the arm.
A blow that is felt tells you that a beast is hurt, but a blow that is understood tells you why, and what to bring next time.
Ariadne gave Theseus more than thread. Those who help you on the road know how the beast at the end of it can be hurt, and they will tell you.
Trust is slow work. Watch how a wary creature greets you each time you come back, for it is telling you whether you make any headway.
A frightened traveller does not heal on the road. Keep the ones you lead close on the stairs and out of the fight.
Swear only what you can carry down, for a promise follows you from floor to floor, and someone farther down is waiting to see whether you kept it.
A beaten creature's trust comes slowly, and never to one who is in a hurry.
Deep in the old mines a little sprite with a glowing bobble still dances alone every night, though a dance needs a partner, and the miners who danced with him always brought tarts.
Who drew the sword, the garter cut, but never blew the bugle-horn: so ends the sleeping king's rhyme, and take care that it is never said of you.
Kill the runner before he reaches his friends, for a goblin who runs is not always fleeing.
Trolls hate the light, for in a lantern's glow a troll's wounds will not close, and the Light spell makes him flinch.
A fire beetle that glows white-hot is about to burst, so step back before the last blow or finish it from afar.
Herodotus says that the gold-diggers of India let a camel go now and then as the ants gained on them, and gold will slow a greedy pursuer as well as a camel does.
A scroll of greater protection turns every arrow aside, seen or unseen.
Confusion of Tongues breaks a war band or a pack into creatures that fight alone.
A dragon's fire is no bottomless well. After it breathes it must draw breath again, but while it does so its claw and bite come at once.
A wight's touch takes life that sleep only half gives back, and a physician or a strong prayer gives back the rest.
4: Odin gave an eye for one drink from Mimir's well. Now and then a trader deep down has a mouthful of it for sale, and the water still asks a price of whoever drinks it.
Legends do not answer to easy philosophy, for the harder a thing was to make, the harder is the question that unmasks it.
Odin's spear has never yet missed what it was thrown at, and it will not begin on your account.
The jackal-god's black sickle feeds upon endings, and each life that it finishes puts a little back into the hand that holds it.
The common spheres hold creatures of sparks, of water, of thorns and of flame.
Traders carry spheres that the dungeon seldom gives up, and a full purse can buy a friend who is already grown.
The hero who killed the dragon did not meet it standing up.
Dragon fire passes over the head of anyone low enough, but the dragon's patience will run out, and he will come looking.
Lay a broken sword on Odin's altar and he will take it politely and give you something to dig with. He once claimed a whole army by throwing a spear over it, and he respects that gesture.
A dead dragon's blood is worth drinking if you know your beasts, and the more of the birds' talk you can follow, the more they will tell you.
Perseus kept only the head, but a good cook might keep rather more, and never fear that kind of stare again.
The wolf grows angrier the longer he is fought, and the gods, who never beat him by strength, bound him with a ribbon.
From a journal found frozen shut: 'He cannot keep his feet on the ice. Why did I fight him on the stone?'
Dwarves bound the wolf with things that do not exist, such as the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard and the roots of a mountain, and someone has left them lying about.
Binding the wolf was never free, for Tyr paid a hand for it, and the ribbon still asks something of whoever holds it.
Scraps that cobblers throw away go into the silent god's shoe, which has been a very long time in the making and was never meant for walking in.
When you light the cold braziers in Fenrir's hall, choose which patches to melt, for ice trips the wolf as surely as it trips you.
Somewhere below lies a worn page in red-brown ink that smells of old fires and bears a single verse. Keep it until you understand whom the verse is about.
An ancient tablet with a hollow in its centre is half of something, and the other half, which shines, is not found until the very end.
Hell's princes each keep a seal and a stair. Neither opens while its keeper lives, and the last stair of all counts every one.
No two of the seal-keepers fight alike, for one grows wrathful once he bleeds, one feeds on the wounds he gives and one never stands still. Learn each before you close with him.
Below the wolf certain floors have a legend living on them and others have none, and the stair will tell you which as you step off it.
Scratched beside a stair, far down: 'The scales give nothing to a soul that weighs nothing either way, and so the lukewarm go on unarmed.'
Only prayer wakes the altar of the scales, and it will wake but once.
An Archangel's scales weigh souls and can do one thing more, for whoever carries them into the last hall does not fight alone.
When the scales call, the Host of Heaven comes, and its quarrel is with the locusts alone.
No one finds the blade of white fire, for it is given only to those who reach the bottom having kept their word, refused what was not theirs and held firm the whole way down.
Your old self may be waiting on the floor where it fell, guarding your old gear, and both gear and owner have gone bad.
Certain altars are not for praying at, and each asks one thing, once. You may walk away freely, but a wrong answer has its price.
Sisyphus left his boulder at the foot of a slope. Take it up and walk, and the hill will count every step that you carry it.
Over a smoking rift sits a priestess who takes coin and answers in riddles about the habits the dungeon rewards, and she costs less than learning them by accident.
Holy books are worth a blessing to the right hands and a purse of gold to the wrong ones, and whoever carries one is asked on the way down which kind of hands he has.
A sealed scroll taken from a named terror is worth more above ground than below. It is meant for a father's eyes.
Jerome kept a lion under his desk and a skull on top of it, and held that a translator who dodges a hard word has told a lie.
A wounded king who is left alone does not stay wounded, so if you walk away from a throne room, expect to start again.
Whatever you mean to do to the bull, do it quickly, for he does not tire but grows angrier.
A clever mind does not make the fire hotter, but makes it last and reach the far side of the room.
Fortune will hand you a few gifts and then close her hand, but what you cook and what you choose she cannot take back.
The scales do not tally every good deed. Each long stretch of the descent is weighed once, so a heap of virtue in one place counts for less than goodness carried the whole way down.
A promise you simply fail to keep is no lie and is not punished as one, yet neither is it a promise kept, and the long count knows the difference.
A floor has one way down, and when you count two, one of them is hungry.
Bring the mirror and the blindfold twice, for Medusa had two sisters, and neither of them can die for long.
A court that lies is owed nothing. To hand yourself, or anyone, to a crooked judge is no courage but only giving up, and the scales count it as nothing more.
An old adventurer scratched a line into a cave wall the way Caesar wrote to his generals: D KROORZ YRLFH VDBV SOXJK.
The Furies need no eyes, for they find the guilty wherever they hide.
In his own labyrinth Asterion always knows where you are, for it is his house.
Thin ice may hold you, but it will not hold you and a heavy pack. Lead a heavy hunter across it in your stead.
Step round the sigils of the Abyss, for they drink the magic of whoever stands on them.
Devils obey their captain out of fear, and if you kill him they will finish the job on each other.
The locusts of the Pit climb out of the smoke, and every vent you shut with a prayer is one they cannot use.
Cobalt steel was forged against the frost and sunsteel in a volcano's throat, and each guards against its own birthplace and is a little afraid of the other's.
Soulsteel was forged to keep a soul in its body, so whatever drinks the life of the living finds it a poor cup.
Adamantine laughs at edges and points, though it weighs like a guilty conscience.
Mithril does not ring or clank, so a thief in a mithril shirt is no louder than a rumour.
Carry a blade, a point and a hammer, for the deeper the dungeon, the more its creatures wear armour of their own: scales that turn an edge, hides that soak a club.
Shepherds on the high fells swear by felted fleece against the frost, as does any armourer who has been where the wolf lives.
A slow traveller is a meal in the deep. Carry what you need and leave the rest for the next fool.
Against a beast that hits like a falling wall, a careful guard is worth more than a bold blow, but it is not so against one that dies quickly.
The heavier the two-handed blade the worse it parries, and a quarterstaff will turn a blow that a maul could only meet.
The water of Siloam's pool opened a blind man's eyes, but dashed on the damned it opens other things.
Medea sent a rival a wedding robe that burst into flame, and her fire, bottled, still works on whatever it touches.
The alkahest was the alchemists' universal solvent, and none could ever say in what jar they kept it.
The master hunter need not think which arrow to draw, for his hand has already chosen.
Know enough of a family and every one of its kin is known to you, even the ones you have never laid on a table.
Hunt a family long enough and it learns your name, and the lesser of its kind would rather run than meet you.
Some families are bound together in the old stories, and if you learn them all the stories give you something back.
A creature that leaves no body behind can still be read, by anyone with the right wand and the nerve to point it.
Even a great beast can be read before it is fought, though it will take no pleasure in it.
The traders who come this deep know better than anyone what waits beneath the stalls, so mind the merchant whose shelves look oddly particular.
A smith's promise is good at his next stall, if you live to reach it. Order the armour you will need and not the armour you wish you had.
Merchants this deep are generous only to customers, and a traveller who sells and never buys is paid a traveller's price.
The quiet of a floor is spent but once, and though a keen mind drinks deeper from it, no mind drinks twice.
Wax in the ears stops a siren's song, and a friend's warning too.
Keep a hammer at your back for creatures that laugh at edges, for a change of hands is quicker than a change of mind.
Deep down a hero dresses for the floor ahead, with one harness for fire and another for frost, and changes on the stair rather than in the fight.
A legend once worn remembers how far you climbed with it, and lets you start there again.
In the frost, a burning brand is worth more than a sharp one.
When Odin's altar speaks of the worm, heed it, for it is not making conversation.
A smith's voice behind an anvil once said that fire bites every wolf, and smiths are seldom wrong about fire.
Holy water poured on a blessed blade is wasted, for Heaven does not bless the same steel twice.
Save your pinch of silver dust for the steel, since a silvered blade needs none.
The dwarf smith of the deep halls will line a cloak against the cold, and she has much to say about your boots.
Basilisk, cockatrice and gorgon all kill with a look, and a mirror answers every one of them.
In a cavern of the deep Underway a loud man in a gold coat races starved birds for bets. The fastest of them will not run a step for him, though for one she trusted she might run like the wind.
The watchman of the gods hears the grass grow and the wool on the sheep, and he trusts his horn only to one who can sit the watch with him and hear what he hears.
A sickness in a wound stops it mending. While you are diseased, rest does nothing and potions and spells heal half: cure it first.
A priest who heals his friends must rest his voice between prayers, so kill him first, or else the one he has just mended.
A lookout that sees you will shout for the rest of its kind, so kill it from afar or never let it see you.
The Serbian smith who blinded Likho escaped beneath a sheepskin, for ill luck that cannot see you cannot follow you.
Zap an archer or a slinger with the Wand of Unstringing and it has to come to you.
Water of Epidaurus gives back every stat point a drain or a disease took.
Jonah came alive out of the great fish, and whatever takes a man whole can be cut open from within.
A bandit captain carries something for a bad day. Make that day a short one, and whatever he saved will be yours.
As any Irishman will tell you, a leprechaun pays only when there is nowhere left for him to run.
5: The Stone waits at the very bottom, in the keeping of the last enemy. Winning it is but half the errand, for afterward you must climb again every stair that you came down.
The Destroyer stands in a darkness that swallows blows, but light is the cure for dark, and in that hall there is light to be had for the asking.
Have your sums ready, for the fire of the altars round the last hall strips the dark from the Destroyer, but never for long.
White fire takes no heed of the Destroyer's darkness, and it hates the things of the Pit above all others. Few come bearing that blade, and the rest must find their light where they stand.
Three roads lead through the last dark, by borrowed fire, by a given sword or by plain stubbornness, and the third is by far the longest.
His locusts rise as fast as they fall, up to a limit that is higher for the wicked, and so the Destroyer never fights alone for long.
A wounded Destroyer is worse than a whole one, so keep something back for the end of the fight.
The weighing comes before the fight, for what the scales found on the floor above decides how strong the Destroyer is and how many he brings.
Just above the bottom you will be weighed by the Archangel whose name is on the white blade, and he has watched you since the first floor.
Honour and cruelty are paid at the bottom in the same coin, for those who kept faith all the way down are armed for the last fight, and the cruel find that it has been armed against them.
Between the sword and the sentence the Archangel keeps several other verdicts, and you choose your own, one stranger at a time.
No saint was ever made in haste, and the honest road through the dungeon is the expensive one, floor after floor.
A seal is never broken by the touching of it, for seals break when their keepers fall.
Nothing down here is truly unkillable, for the old songs give every such creature a heel, and the dungeon has kept the songs.
Death does not wait at the bottom, but sets out when the Stone starts upward. He is slow in the deep and quicker with every stretch of the climb, and near the surface he is faster than you.
On the last page of a climber's journal was written: 'His speed buys him distance, but not blows. The scythe falls only on those who stop beside him, as I have stopped to write this.'
Prayer cannot kill Death, but it can make him wait, and at an altar he waits longer.
Stop time if you have the means, though one traveller on the stairs behind you will pay it no heed.
On one of the early floors the ground shimmers and quotes a verse at whoever stands there. Though nothing comes of it then, remember the place.
A Stone of legend and a Tablet of legend are two halves of one key, though neither knows it, and they are joined by something very ordinary from a workman's belt.
The last book tells what becomes of Death at the end, and one scroll down here carries that line. It matters greatly where the reader stands when he reads it, and who stands there with him.
Only in one place may Death be ended, and since it lies near the top, where he also runs fastest, you should arrive with the work already done.
Long before this dungeon there was a cave game with a nonsense word that carried the player somewhere else, and people have been typing it into things ever since.
One great plea is answered, once and finally. From an altar its question is gentle, but from anywhere else there are several, and none of them is gentle.
Heaven does not take a careless great plea kindly. Afterward, look to what you are wearing, if you still have eyes to see it.
Whoever names enough things truly is changed by the naming, first with a quicker mind, later with a sharper eye, and at the very last with something to wear. The count is long, so start early.
A companion changes its whole shape as it grows, though most companions never live to see the last change.
Thor's belt of strength gives its wearer what the songs promise, and makes him quicker into the bargain.
Andvari's ring was cursed to ruin every owner it ever had, but the one down here has mellowed, and the gold that it once made still finds its way to the hand that wears it.
By the bottom you will have several times the thinking time with which you began, and you will have need of every second.
Rest will close a wound only so far, and the last of your strength comes back at the table, from a bottle or upon your knees.
A hint is a riddle rather than a recipe, and the dungeon trusts you to do the rest of the work.
When the well of lore runs dry, let it fill again, for memory, like any spring, needs a while between buckets.
If two hints seem to quarrel, they are likely speaking of different travellers, for the dungeon is large enough for both.
A right deed done once makes a good day. The same deed done again, stretch after stretch, grows into character, and it is character that the Archangel weighs.
Kindness without judgment is a coin tossed into the dark. Look first and ask before you give, for the careful hand is the one that the scales remember.
A small cut makes two of what bleeds salt, but one great blow does not divide it.
Keep your own heart light, for deep down there are jaws that weigh the heart before they bite.
The last thing a hunter learns of a family is the thing it most fears in him.
If you know enough families to their last secret, the dungeon will call you by a new name.
The Destroyer wears fire, frost and venom like old clothes. What is holy he has never learned to bear.
The climb back up is longer than the descent, and with each ounce you carry Death gains upon you a little more quickly.
Against the last enemy the bold blow and the careful guard are both right, each in its moment, so learn to know which moment it is.
By the bottom you should own an answer to every trick a monster knows. Keep a mirror, a pinch of wax and a nail of cold iron, even when they weigh upon you.
Read the Destroyer before you fight him, if you can, for his is the last page that your book will need.
A great wizard at the bottom of the world carries little iron and a great deal of quiet.
At the bottom each creature is master of its own one craft, and a coat that is good against everything is good against nothing in particular.
A wise hunter spends his last charge of reading on a beast he has never met, rather than on one that he has already buried.
Oliver begged Roland to sound his horn while the emperor was still near, but Roland was too proud and help came too late. Call for help early, then give ground until it comes.
When a necromancer begins to chant, strike him. A blow breaks the chant, and he must begin his calling again.
The Water of the Styx turns every blow, bite and claw, but an unseen blow finds the heel.
Demons cannot strike you up close while the Udug Hul holds, until you strike one.
A spell takes a breath to say, and a blow struck in that breath is worth two that are struck after it.
The dead in their mounds guard only what is their own, so if you leave the barrow, the barrow lets you go.
Stand beside a fire elemental or a frost giant and you burn or freeze, though neither has struck you.
